newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels free more hostages from Japan embassy.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels free more hostages from Japan embassy.

text.p: Peruvian guerrillas holding 400 hostages at the the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima released another 38 captives on Friday night, Red Cross officials said.

At least 25 men were seen walking out of the compound into the street escorted by Red Cross officials. One of them was being pushed in a wheelchair. Red Cross mediator Michel Minning said 38 victims were being freed in total.
The release was the first from the besieged residence since a smaller number of hostages were set free on Thursday.
"I have just been informed ... that 25 hostages have just been released," Anthony Vincent, Canada's ambassador to Peru, told Canadian Broadcasting Corp. television in an interview from Lima.
The Peruvian government ignored desperate pleas by the hostages for vital services to be restored to the besieged residence as the hostage crisis neared its fourth day.

Neither handwritten signs thrust at a residence window requesting water, electricity and telephone service in four languages nor reports of worsening hostage health appeared to move President Alberto Fujimori.

As Peruvians prayed for the lives of the captives, their president spent much of the day huddled with generals at a military barracks. His government has so far rejected all the Marxist hostage-takers' demands, most notably their request for jailed comrades to be set free.

Around 20 heavily armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels stormed from jungle obscurity onto the world's front pages by taking over the Japanese residence on Tuesday night during a smart reception.
Three days after their daring assault, they still held their hostages in worsening health, including more than a dozen ambassadors, two Peruvian Cabinet ministers and about 40 Japanese businessmen.
Red Cross officials said some of the captives were suffering from diarrhoea, diabetes, ulcers and heart problems, but there was no sign that the rebels would let them go.
Citizens across this poor Andean nation clustered around radio sets and televisions in bars, shops and cafes hungrily seeking the latest word on the hostages' fate.
Japan and the United States both pushed Peru to seek a peaceful solution to the crisis and put hostages' lives first, using a cautious, go-slow approach in negotiations.
Fujimori assured President Bill Clinton he would do so, but the true intentions of the enigmatic Peruvian leader, better known for strong-arm tactics than diplomacy, were unclear.

His prime minister, Alberto Pandolfi, kept hopes up by telling reporters the government hoped for a peaceful end to the crisis, but police sources said preparations for a commando-style raid were being considered as part of a range of options.
Both the United States and Britain have sent security experts to Peru in case their help is needed.
Under international law, the besieged residence is considered Japanese territory so Fujimori must seek Tokyo's permission before taking any military action.

Negotiations by the Red Cross and a team of diplomats over the past two days appeared to have achieved little more than getting food, water and much-needed portable toilets into the besieged residence.

Red Cross workers ferried in containers of water, soft drinks, salads, cake and medicines to the portals of the elegant residence on Friday morning, but there was no visible progress toward ending the siege.

Inside, the hostages -- who include Peru's anti-terrorism chief and its foreign minister -- faced their fourth straight night sleeping on the floor in crumpled suits and sharing meagre rations under the watchful gaze of their captors.
Adding to the tension, a man claiming to be an MRTA guerrilla phoned Lima's CPN radio station to warn authorities against risking any commando raid on the residence.
"We don't want any attack or any assault," the unidentified caller said. "We know we're dead anyway, and there's nothing left but for us all to die together."
Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent, one of a group of envoys released on Wednesday to act as mediators, told reporters on Friday evening that their humanitarian mission had ended.
"The ambassadors state that they have now completed their mission," he said, adding that he remained "committed to the well-being and safety of the hostages."
Anxious relatives, some of whom prayed through the night for captives, waited outside in the hope of news. A big candle-lit vigil was planned for the evening in a park near the residence.
Earlier in the day police had to turn back hordes of family members from the crowded streets outside the residence as they tried to donate medicine, blankets and food.
The relatives were told to channel assistance through the Red Cross, which is mediating between the rebels and the official government negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo.

Ikeda seemed to have little to show for 20 hours of nonstop diplomacy. His agenda included talks with the large Japanese community, the Canadian mediator and the U.S. ambassador but no fresh talks with Fujimori, whom he saw briefly on arrival on Thursday night.

So far Fujimori's hard line against the rebels seemed popular with ordinary Peruvians, who are fed up with guerrilla violence. Citizens up and down the country hoisted national flags on makeshift masts or draped them from windows to show their support for the government.
